The concept of entropy, first introduced in the 19th century through the study of thermodynamics, has since transcended its original boundaries to become a cornerstone of multiple disciplines. In physics, entropy is often described as a measure of disorder, reflecting the tendency of systems to evolve from order to chaos. However, in information theory, pioneered by Claude Shannon, entropy takes on a different meaning: it quantifies uncertainty in a message and determines the efficiency of data compression. Despite the difference in application, both interpretations converge on the idea of unpredictability and the irreversible nature of certain processes. Beyond science and engineering, entropy has been adopted as a metaphor in philosophy, economics, and even cultural studies. For instance, economists use entropy to describe the inevitable decline of markets without corrective inputs, while philosophers invoke it to highlight the fragility of structured systems in human societies. This interdisciplinary usage underscores the universal relevance of entropy: whether in the breakdown of a physical system, the degradation of information, or the disintegration of institutions, entropy symbolizes the inexorable drift towards disorder. Yet, it is important to note that entropy is not merely destructive; it also drives change, adaptation, and innovation, as systems reorganize to resist or harness it.
